chapter: New York with Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins
title: Capitol recordings: April in Paris, and Stuffy as his first solo identification
summary: Thompson recalls Capitol's Hollywood Stampede ballads and April in Paris, and Stuffy, born from group ideas with Hawkins, credited to the leader, and loved by Hawkins and Roy Eldridge.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Particularly the ballads. I thought they were very good. We recorded "April in Paris", which was over recorded after that in many fashions, but it was later made famous by Bill Davis on the organ and Count Basie. One More Time.

"April in Paris" arrangement. But we had a beautiful arrangement that went on that, featuring Coleman Hawkins on those recordings of Capitol. And I had a song also that I had a little something to do with during that time which brought out my first solo identification, believe it or not, in that band. It's the first time that I came to be known as a solo player with my own style, which brought out this style of playing that I had, which was my own, and later on become recognized as me. And that was a piece called "Stuffy" Stuffing.
Yes, I think I remember that. That was an up tempo, wasn't it?
That's right, that's it. That was your number too?

Yes,well, see, these are the kind of things -- these kind of creations,musicians -- we got these things together as a group. Maybe I would have an idea, and Coleman Hawkins would have an idea, we'd get it together and make a piece out of it, see. And of course in some cases where it was done as a group the leader would get credit for being a composer, and so forth and so on, so forth. And I didn't get any credit for it, in fact I didn't consider myself as being the author of that piece, but we all had something to do with making it a hit. And it was one of the famous records out of that album.
In fact it was the most famous, I believe, of those recordings which later became almost like a theme song to Coleman and Roy Eldridge, who loved to play that song.
And I was very flattered that they used to play my solo together.
I'd like to hum it for you now.
The first solo I played that I was identified with as a jazz player --
